book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Iron — How Jyoti Makes & Sells Precision Machines
question: What exactly does Jyoti CNC build, how does its product mix shift across 3-axis and 5-axis tiers, and which end-markets drive its ₹5,082 crore order book?

epigraph.quote: Machine tools are the mother machines of industry: every turbine blade, gearbox housing, and smartphone chassis begins as raw metal shaped by a spindle.
epigraph.author: Precision Manufacturing Primer

web_blocks.html: Jyoti CNC Automation designs, builds, and services Computer Numerical Control (CNC) metal-cutting machine tools [1][4][19]. Its catalog spans entry-level 2-axis turning centers and 3-axis vertical machining centers (VMCs) [1][4]. It also makes ultra-precision simultaneous 5-axis machines, turn-mill centers, and robotic cells [1][4][19]. Across India's CNC market, Jyoti holds roughly an 8% to 10% overall share [1][15]. It ranks among the top domestic builders alongside Ace Micromatic Group and Bharat Fritz Werner (BFW) [1][15]. In domestic simultaneous 5-axis systems, Jyoti commands clear leadership [1][15].

web_blocks.title: Product Portfolio & Average Selling Price (ASP) Ladder

web_blocks.html: A CNC builder's economics depend heavily on where a machine sits on the axis ladder. At the base are high-volume turning centers (DX and AX series) and compact VMCs [4]. MSME auto-component job shops buy these units for cost-sensitive work [4]. In the middle sit horizontal machining centers (HMCs), twin-spindle systems (TS series), and heavy die-mould machines [4]. Auto and industrial plants run them across three shifts [4]. At the top sit simultaneous 5-axis and double-column gantry systems [2][19][20]. Anchored by the Huron GU5 Five, KX, and U-Mill lines, they use 18,000 RPM electro-spindles and hold micron-level accuracy [2][19][20]. These top-tier systems carry much higher Average Selling Prices (ASPs) and gross margins [2][19]. Consolidated gross margin reached 55.1% in FY26 as material costs fell to 48.00% of sales [2]. In Q2 FY27, Jyoti shipped ~1,911 machines against ₹602 crore in consolidated sales [5][20]. That implies a blended realization near ₹31.5 lakh per machine [5][20]. Individual 2-axis lathes sell for far less, while custom 5-axis aerospace gantries sell for multiples of that figure [5][20].

web_blocks.takeaway: Moving customers up the ladder from 2-axis lathes to 5-axis simultaneous machining centers expands gross margins (55.1% in FY26) but lengthens build cycles from weeks to 3–18 months.

web_blocks.title: Customer End-Markets & Order Book Anatomy (₹5,082 Crore)

web_blocks.html: By September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27), Jyoti CNC's consolidated order book hit ₹5,082 crore, up from ₹4,848 crore in Q1 FY27 [1][5]. That backlog equals roughly 2.2x trailing-twelve-month sales of ₹2,286 crore [1][5]. Aerospace & Defence accounts for ~38% to 41% of the total backlog [5][14]. Quarterly order intake, however, stays balanced across four distinct industrial buyer groups [5][14]:

1. Automotive & Auto Components (~50% of Q2 FY27 intake): Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers in Pune, Chennai, NCR, and Gujarat buy DX/AX turning centers and TS twin-spindle systems [4][5]. They machine transmission shafts, EV motor housings, and precision bearings [4][5]. These orders ship fast and smooth out plant utilization. 2. General Engineering (~27% of Q2 FY27 intake): Pump, valve, capital-equipment, and gearbox makers buy heavy-duty HMCs and VMCs for multi-shift runs [4][5]. 3. Electronics Manufacturing Services / EMS (~13% of Q2 FY27 intake): Contract assemblers expanding Indian smartphone and electronics output order banks of high-speed Tachyon and PX VMCs [4][5]. Synchronized cells mill precision aluminum chassis and enclosures [4][5]. 4. Aerospace & Defence (~38–41% of total backlog): Airframe, satellite, and defence buyers order Huron GU5 Five and KX 5-axis gantries on 3-to-18 month build cycles [7][14][20]. Total Q2 FY27 inflows topped ₹800 crore [5][6]. Auto and general engineering led quarterly intake while lumpy aerospace tenders shifted timelines, yet defence orders still anchor multi-year visibility [5][6].

web_blocks.title: Captive Foundry, Unit Scale-Up & The MeitY ECMS Backward Integration

web_blocks.html: Unit execution is scaling fast on the shop floor. Jyoti shipped a record ~1,911 machines in Q2 FY27 against a full-year FY27 goal above 8,000 units [5][6][12]. At the same time, a ₹400–450 crore Rajkot expansion is lifting annual capacity from 6,000 to 16,000 machines [5][6][12]. Jyoti runs a 1,500–2,000 metric tonne/month captive Meehanite foundry at Metoda, Rajkot [4]. Pouring its own beds, columns, and saddles gives it tight control over vibration damping and thermal stability [4]. Like all Indian CNC builders, however, Jyoti still relies on imported Fanuc (Japan) and Siemens (Germany) controllers, servo drives, and motors [6]. Global lead times for those electronics more than doubled in 2026 [6]. To cut that bottleneck, Jyoti won Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) approval under the Electronic Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) [12]. The ₹1,020.65 crore multi-year program will localize domestic CNC electronics and controllers [12].

These four buyer groups show very different cash and margin profiles. Standard DX/AX lathes and Tachyon/PX VMC cells for Auto (~50% of Q2 FY27 intake) and EMS (~13% of intake) turn over quickly [4][5]. They use standard castings and repeatable assembly bays [4][5]. By contrast, Aerospace & Defence systems (~38–41% of the ₹5,082 crore backlog) require custom fixturing [7][14][20]. They also demand 18,000 RPM spindle run-in tests and multi-month buyer acceptance trials before dispatch [7][14][20]. That mix shift explains why consolidated gross margin reached 55.1% in FY26 even as build cycles lengthened [2][7].

web_blocks.title: Why Customers Buy Simultaneous 5-Axis Instead of 3-Axis Machines
paragraphs: A 3-axis VMC moves a tool along X, Y, and Z linear planes. To cut the underside or angled pockets of an aerospace bracket, an operator must unclamp, re-fixture, and re-zero the part several times. Each reset adds human and alignment error.

A simultaneous 5-axis machine adds two rotary axes that tilt and rotate the table or spindle head. The tool can reach a titanium or aluminum billet from almost any angle in one setup. This cuts cycle times by 40–60% and holds single-digit micron tolerances, so Aerospace & Defence and die-mould buyers accept 3-to-18 month delivery schedules [7][20].

book_paragraphs: To understand why Jyoti CNC's order book sits above ₹5,000 crore while its inventory sits above 450 days, you and I need to walk the factory floor at Metoda and Lodhika GIDC on the outskirts of Rajkot. Outside, Gujarat's sun bakes the highway; inside, molten iron is pouring into sand moulds inside Jyoti's captive foundry at a pace of 1,500 to 2,000 tonnes every month. Most casual observers think a CNC machine is a software product. It isn't. First and foremost, it is a massive, stress-relieved block of cast iron engineered not to vibrate by even a thousandth of a millimeter while a carbide tool rips through titanium at 18,000 revolutions per minute.

That captive foundry is where Jyoti's business model begins. By pouring and seasoning its own machine beds, columns, and saddles in Rajkot rather than buying castings from third-party jobbers, Jyoti controls both metallurgical damping quality and delivery schedules. From the foundry, those raw castings travel through heavy milling bays, hand-scraping stations—where master technicians literally scrape guideways by hand to achieve micron-level flatness—into climate-controlled assembly halls where spindles, ball screws, linear motion guides, and sheet-metal enclosures come together. Today, management is investing ₹400 crore to ₹450 crore to expand that Rajkot footprint from 6,000 machines a year to 16,000 machines, after dispatching a record 1,911 units in Q2 FY27 alone against a full-year goal of over 8,000 machines.

If you divide ₹602 crore of Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue by those 1,911 dispatched machines, you get an average blended realization of roughly ₹31.5 lakh per unit. But averages hide the real economics! A CNC machine builder's margins depend entirely on where a machine sits on the axis-and-rigidity ladder. Now picture the four distinct types of customers walking through those assembly halls, because each one buys a completely different tier of machine.

The first customer is the workhorse of Indian manufacturing: an auto-component or bearing supplier in Pune, Chennai, or Rajkot buying a standard 2-axis DX turning center or a twin-spindle TS machine to carve transmission shafts and EV motor housings around the clock. These machines ship quickly, carry modest selling prices, and compete head-to-head with Ace Micromatic and Macpower on uptime, service speed, and total cost of ownership. In Q2 FY27, automotive and auto components alone drove roughly half of Jyoti's ₹800-plus crore in fresh order inflows—keeping the Rajkot assembly lines humming.

The second customer is the general engineering and industrial machinery buyer—accounting for around 27% of Q2 FY27 inflows—ordering horizontal machining centers and heavy vertical mills to machine pumps, valves, and industrial gearboxes twenty-four hours a day. Here, structural rigidity and low downtime decide repeat orders.

The third customer is India's newest structural growth engine: Electronics Manufacturing Services, or EMS, representing 13% of Q2 FY27 intake. Walk into a smartphone-enclosure plant in Tamil Nadu or Karnataka and you won't see one machine—you'll see long rows of identical, high-speed Tachyon and PX vertical machining centers running in synchronized cells, carving thousands of ultra-thin aluminum chassis every shift. Speed, rapid tool-changing, and spindle reliability are everything, and when an EMS giant expands a factory line, it orders machines by the dozen.

The fourth customer is the crown jewel—and the source of both Jyoti's highest margins and its longest working-capital lockup: Aerospace and Defence. Representing roughly 38% to 41% of the total ₹5,082 crore backlog (up from ₹4,848 crore in Q1 FY27), these buyers aren't ordering standard catalog lathes. They are ordering simultaneous 5-axis machining centers and double-column Huron GU5 Five and KX gantries to mill aircraft structural ribs, turbine blades, and missile components. In a standard 3-axis machine, an operator has to stop, unclamp, and flip a complex billet to cut another face, risking micron-level misalignment. In a 5-axis machine, the table tilts and rotates continuously while an 18,000 RPM spindle carves an impeller blade in one uninterrupted setup. That complexity pushed Jyoti's consolidated gross margin to 55.1% in FY26, with raw materials consuming just 48.00% of revenue.

Think about the practical shop-floor difference between those four customer types. When an auto-component shop orders ten DX turning centers or an EMS plant orders a bank of Tachyon VMCs, Jyoti's engineers assemble them on repeatable lines using standardized castings and ship them within weeks. When an aerospace contractor orders a Huron 5-axis gantry, however, Jyoti's application engineers must design custom fixturing, run multi-week thermal and volumetric calibration tests, and host customer inspection teams for trial cuts before the machine ever leaves the floor. That is why CRISIL highlights 3-to-18 month manufacturing cycles on specialized multi-axis orders—and why high-margin aerospace work naturally slows down inventory turnover.

Here is the catch you and I must keep front and center: every CNC machine still needs a digital 'brain'—the CNC controller, servo drives, and feedback encoders. Today, Jyoti builds the iron, the sheet metal, and increasingly its own spindles, but the electronic brain still comes largely from Fanuc in Japan or Siemens in Germany. When global controller lead times more than doubled in 2026, Jyoti had to hoard imported controllers and sub-assemblies in advance just to protect its Q2 FY27 dispatches of 1,911 machines. That is why management secured MeitY's ₹1,020.65 crore ECMS approval to build CNC electronics in-house over the coming years—an ambitious bet to turn a heavy metal bender into a true mechatronics company.

Pause for a moment to appreciate why that captive foundry and electronics roadmap fit together like two halves of a single puzzle. In Rajkot, Jyoti already controls the heavy iron—pouring 1,500 to 2,000 metric tonnes of Meehanite castings a month, seasoning them, and machining its own beds and columns. That mechanical vertical integration is what lets Jyoti serve both high-volume auto-component buyers and precision aerospace contractors under one roof. Yet until Jyoti also masters the electronic brain, its assembly lines remain at the mercy of overseas controller allocations.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A 5-axis aerospace order book is a double-edged sword. It lifts gross margins to 55.1% and creates high switching costs, because once an aerospace supplier qualifies a Huron or Jyoti machine for a fuselage part, changing builders requires costly re-certification. Yet that very customization—combined with imported Fanuc/Siemens controllers and 3-to-18 month build cycles—is what traps hundreds of crores inside work-in-progress inventory.

book_callouts.title: THE MECHATRONICS BET
book_callouts.text: Watch the ₹1,020.65 crore MeitY ECMS electronics program closely. If Jyoti successfully localizes controllers and servo drives, it reduces its reliance on Fanuc and Siemens lead times; if execution slips, that capex will weigh on returns before it relieves working capital.

book_callouts.title: ORDER BOOK VISIBILITY VS. LUMPINESS
book_callouts.text: Notice how Q2 FY27 order intake (>₹800 crore) was led 50% by Auto and 27% by General Engineering while Aerospace tenders shifted timelines—even though Aerospace & Defence still makes up 38–41% of the ₹5,082 crore backlog. That two-speed engine keeps factories busy between lumpy defence awards.
